Saudi Arabia Shuts Critical Oil Pipeline as Houthi Forces Tighten Grip on Red Sea Shipping

By Newzyy Staff — 45m ago

Saudi Arabia has temporarily shut down its strategically important East-West oil pipeline following a drone attack, as Iran-aligned Houthi forces continue to expand their control along Yemen’s Red Sea coast.

The simultaneous developments have raised fresh concerns over global energy supplies and international shipping, particularly as major routes through the Middle East are already facing severe disruption.

The latest escalation is putting additional pressure on Saudi Arabia, one of the world’s largest oil exporters, while global markets are closely watching whether the disruption to oil and shipping routes will continue.

The East-West pipeline, also known as the Petroline, stretches approximately 1,200 kilometres across Saudi Arabia, connecting the kingdom’s oil-producing areas in the east with the Red Sea port of Yanbu. The route allows Saudi Arabia to transport crude toward the Red Sea without relying entirely on tanker traffic through the Strait of Hormuz.

Saudi Arabia shuts down key oil route

Saudi authorities said the pipeline was temporarily shut down as a precaution after several drones struck infrastructure in the Riyadh and Madinah regions.

The attacks caused damage and injuries, prompting emergency and technical teams to secure the affected facilities and assess the condition of the pipeline.

Saudi officials said the drones originated from Iraq. Riyadh has so far chosen not to launch an immediate retaliation against Baghdad, giving the Iraqi government an opportunity to investigate the incident and take action against those responsible.

The attack has created a major problem for Saudi Arabia because the East-West pipeline has become increasingly important as an alternative route for exporting crude while shipping through the Strait of Hormuz remains heavily disrupted.

Why the pipeline is so important

The East-West pipeline is one of Saudi Arabia’s most important pieces of energy infrastructure.

It provides a land-based route across the Arabian Peninsula, allowing Saudi crude to reach the Red Sea and international markets without having to travel through the Strait of Hormuz.

According to Reuters, the pipeline had been carrying around 4 million to 5 million barrels of oil per day, representing roughly 4% to 5% of global oil supply. Other reports have cited a higher maximum capacity, meaning the potential significance of the route is even greater if the disruption becomes prolonged.

With the pipeline now offline, Saudi Arabia has fewer options for moving crude to international customers.

Houthi forces expand along Red Sea coast

The pipeline attack comes at the same time as a major Houthi advance in Yemen.

Iran-aligned Houthi forces have rapidly expanded their presence along Yemen’s Red Sea coastline and have taken control of strategically important areas, including the port city of Mokha and the nearby Perim Island, also known as Mayun Island.

Perim Island sits in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a critical maritime chokepoint connecting the Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden.

Its location gives it considerable strategic importance because ships travelling between Europe and Asia through the Red Sea and Suez Canal pass through this wider maritime corridor.

The Houthi advance has therefore raised concerns that commercial shipping could face another major disruption if the group attempts to restrict or threaten vessels using the waterway.

Pressure on global shipping

The developments are particularly significant for international trade.

The Red Sea and Bab el-Mandeb have historically been among the world's most important shipping routes, connecting Asian and European markets.

Any prolonged security threat could force shipping companies to avoid the area and take longer routes around Africa. Such diversions can increase fuel consumption, insurance costs and delivery times.

The latest developments are therefore not only a Middle Eastern security issue. They could also affect the cost of transporting goods around the world.

Oil prices react to growing supply concerns

Global oil markets have reacted strongly to the worsening security situation.

Brent crude has risen above $100 per barrel, reflecting growing concerns over disruptions to production, transportation and export routes.

The closure of Saudi Arabia’s East-West pipeline adds another layer of uncertainty because the pipeline had provided an important alternative to the Strait of Hormuz.

If the pipeline remains closed for an extended period while shipping through the Red Sea also becomes increasingly risky, traders could face concerns about how much Gulf oil can reliably reach international markets.

Higher crude prices could eventually feed into higher fuel, transportation and manufacturing costs in countries that depend heavily on imported energy.

Iraq faces pressure after attack

The drone attack has also placed Iraq under increasing political pressure.

Iraqi authorities confirmed that the drones came from Iraqi territory and announced an investigation into the incident.

The government has also taken action against senior security officials as it faces questions over its ability to control armed groups operating inside the country.

An umbrella organization representing Iran-aligned Iraqi militias has denied responsibility for the attack.

The incident highlights the increasingly complicated regional conflict, where several Iran-aligned groups are operating across different countries and targeting strategic infrastructure and routes.

Saudi Arabia seeks greater US support

The growing threats have also increased pressure on Saudi Arabia to strengthen its military and security cooperation with the United States.

Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman has sought American assistance as the kingdom faces simultaneous threats to its oil infrastructure and maritime trade routes.

Washington has indicated that intelligence assistance may be provided, while the United States remains cautious about becoming more deeply involved in another major military escalation in the region.

A wider energy crisis could deepen

The combination of the pipeline shutdown, Houthi advances and continued instability around major Middle Eastern waterways has created an increasingly difficult situation for global energy markets.

Saudi Arabia has traditionally relied on its large oil production capacity and multiple export routes to maintain its position as a major supplier to the global market.

But if both land-based and maritime export routes remain under pressure, the kingdom could face greater difficulties moving crude to customers.

The situation also creates risks for countries across Asia and Europe that rely heavily on oil imports from the Gulf.

What happens next

For now, Saudi authorities are assessing the damage to the East-West pipeline while Iraqi officials investigate the origin of the drone attack.

At the same time, the Houthi advance along Yemen’s Red Sea coast is being closely monitored by regional governments and international shipping companies.

The biggest question is whether the latest disruptions will remain temporary or develop into a longer-lasting threat to global energy supplies and international trade.

Any additional attacks on Saudi energy infrastructure, further Houthi territorial gains or attacks on commercial vessels could push oil prices higher and create even greater pressure on global shipping.

The situation remains highly fluid, with the possibility of further military escalation still a major concern for governments, energy companies and financial markets around the world.
